analysis.architecture_style: Java EE monolith (single EAR) on a WebLogic cluster with PL/SQL-heavy Oracle
analysis.summary: A 180k-line Java 7 / EJB 3.0 application with a JSF 1.2 UI, packaged as one EAR on a 4-node WebLogic 10.3.6 cluster and backed by a 1.2 TB Oracle 11g database with significant PL/SQL. Five integrations mix SOAP, SFTP, nightly Quartz ETL and LDAP. Because everything ships as one EAR, every release requires full re-validation, which drives the 6-month release cycle.

dimensions.rationale: Ant builds, no automated tests and a 6-month validated release cycle.

risks.title: Business logic locked in PL/SQL
risks.description: Core rules live in Oracle packages, so moving engines or extracting services can change validated behaviour.
risks.mitigation: Keep Oracle (managed) during replatform; extract services only behind characterisation tests.

risks.title: Audit trail continuity during data migration
risks.description: Inspection-ready audit trails must survive the migration complete and unaltered.
risks.mitigation: Validated migration with row counts and hash reconciliation of audit tables; QA review before go-live.

risks.title: Disruption to studies in database lock
risks.description: Two studies lock their databases in Q1; cutover then would jeopardise submissions.
risks.mitigation: Schedule cutover after Q1 lock; freeze changes for locking studies.

risks.title: EU subject data leaving the EU
risks.description: A single US-hosted deployment would breach residency commitments for EU subjects.
risks.mitigation: Deploy in an EU region with region-restricting guardrails; document transfers in the DPIA.

risks.title: Full re-validation for every release persists
risks.description: Without modular releases and automated tests, the cloud move alone will not shorten the 6-month cycle.
risks.mitigation: Adopt CSA, automate regression OQ, and validate extracted services independently.

risks.title: Container and Kubernetes skills gap
risks.description: The team knows WebLogic, not containers, EKS or IaC.
risks.mitigation: Pair with a partner for the first two waves; platform team owns golden pipelines.

risks.title: Oracle licensing on cloud
risks.description: Licence terms for Oracle on cloud can raise costs unexpectedly.
risks.mitigation: Use licence-included managed Oracle and right-size; plan a later move of new services to PostgreSQL.

risks.title: APAC site latency persists
risks.description: Moving the same server-rendered UI to one region keeps APAC slow.
risks.mitigation: Serve the new UI from a CDN and keep APIs chatty-free.

opportunities.title: Monthly instead of 6-monthly releases
opportunities.benefit: Independently validated services and automated OQ shrink the release cycle.

opportunities.title: Drop WebLogic licences
opportunities.benefit: Open-source Jakarta EE runtime on containers removes WebLogic licence cost.

opportunities.title: Faster experience for global sites
opportunities.benefit: A CDN-served UI improves performance in 25 countries.

opportunities.title: Inspection readiness on demand
opportunities.benefit: Centralised immutable audit logs make inspection evidence quick to produce.

opportunities.title: Self-service site onboarding
opportunities.benefit: Federated identity with MFA replaces manual site-user management.

plan.headline: Refactor TrialHub in about a year: first replatform the EAR to containers and managed Oracle on AWS, then strangle out site-management and monitoring services - validating each increment so releases drop from 6-monthly to monthly.

patterns.name: Strangler fig
patterns.why: Carve services out of the EAR one domain at a time, validating each small increment instead of the whole system.

patterns.name: Replatform to managed PaaS
patterns.why: Exit end-of-life WebLogic, Java 7 and Oracle 11g first while keeping PL/SQL logic intact.

patterns.name: API gateway facade
patterns.why: Decouples the EDC SOAP contract from EJBs and routes traffic between legacy and new services.

patterns.name: GxP landing zone
patterns.why: EU-resident, policy-guarded accounts with immutable audit logging for an inspected GCP system.

component_strategies.rationale: Replace JSF/RichFaces with a modern SPA served from a CDN for global sites, module by module.
Containerise the EAR on an open-source Jakarta EE runtime first, then extract site and monitoring services.
Licence-included managed Oracle keeps PL/SQL unchanged; new services get their own PostgreSQL schemas.
Move batch out of the app server into observable, retryable managed pipelines.
Vendor system stays; an API facade decouples its SOAP contract.
Vendor keeps SFTP; the endpoint moves to a managed service.
Out of scope; receives data from the new pipeline.
Federated identity with MFA for staff and external site users.

compliance.headline: TrialHub stays inspection-ready through strangler-fig refactoring and risk-based CSA; main compliance work is audit-trail continuity, 25-year TMF retention, EU subject-data residency and multi-vendor supplier qualification.

gaps.title: Inspection-ready audit trail must survive the Oracle migration
gaps.description: Part 11 audit tables are an inspection-grade GCP record. Any migration that drops time-zone metadata, re-sequences rows or recreates sequences invalidates evidence.
gaps.mitigation: Hash and row-count reconciliation of every audit table; validated migration pipeline under change control; QA sign-off on the Data Migration Verification Report before cutover.
gaps.validation_activity: OQ on migrated audit tables + Data Migration Verification Report

gaps.title: 25-year TMF record retention and archive accessibility
gaps.description: Trial master file records must remain readable and accessible for 25 years from study end, through infrastructure changes.
gaps.mitigation: Long-term archive on object storage with lifecycle policies; annual archive-restore drill as part of periodic review.
gaps.validation_activity: Archive IQ and annual restore test documented

gaps.title: EU subject data must stay in the EU
gaps.description: Pseudonymised subject enrolment data for EU sites is GDPR special category. A single US-hosted deployment would breach residency commitments.
gaps.mitigation: Deploy EU workloads in an EU AWS region (eu-west-1 or eu-central-1); apply SCP region allow-list guardrail; update DPIA; document any legitimate cross-border flows.
gaps.validation_activity: Infrastructure IQ confirms region guardrail; DPIA updated

gaps.title: Modular releases require independently validated services
gaps.description: The target monthly-release ambition only holds if each extracted service validates independently, under a CSA / GAMP 5 approach rather than full-system re-validation.
gaps.mitigation: Per-service URS/FS/IQ/OQ artefacts with traceability; automated OQ as the primary test evidence; QA release per service; periodic review per service.

gaps.title: AWS and SaaS vendors must be qualified as GxP suppliers
gaps.description: EDC and IRT vendors are already qualified; AWS and any new managed services need the same treatment, with shared-responsibility documentation.
gaps.mitigation: Use AWS GxP compliance guidance and audit reports (SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001); quality agreement; add AWS to the supplier register with periodic review.
gaps.validation_activity: AWS Supplier Assessment Report + Quality Agreement

gaps.title: External site users managed manually without MFA
gaps.description: Site users today are manually provisioned without MFA. Federated identity with MFA closes an access-control gap for a system holding Part 11 records.
gaps.mitigation: Federated identity via Cognito with external IdP; MFA for site users; self-service onboarding workflow with site-manager approval.
gaps.validation_activity: OQ on identity flow including MFA; access-matrix periodic review

gaps.title: CI/CD pipelines must stay under change control
gaps.description: Automated infrastructure and application pipelines are a change path and must be governed; today's manual process has implicit traceability through CAB records that automation must preserve.
gaps.mitigation: Protected branches, QA approval gates on production deploys, traceable change-ticket -> commit -> artefact chain; pipeline definitions versioned and reviewed.
gaps.validation_activity: CI/CD pipeline qualification (IQ) and periodic review

required_controls.name: Immutable, centrally retained audit logs
required_controls.description: Centralise application and database audit events to CloudWatch Logs with cross-account aggregation and retention sized to the 25-year TMF requirement.

required_controls.name: Region-restriction guardrails
required_controls.description: AWS SCPs enforcing EU-only regions for Cork workloads; cross-region replication only to EU.

required_controls.name: Qualified landing zone
required_controls.description: Multi-account GxP landing zone built from version-controlled IaC with change control; infrastructure qualified via IQ.

required_controls.name: Federated identity with MFA
required_controls.description: Cognito + corporate IdP with MFA for staff and sites; access matrix reviewed every six months.

required_controls.name: Vendor supplier register updated for AWS
required_controls.description: AWS listed with quality agreement, shared-responsibility matrix and periodic review cadence; same treatment for any new SaaS.

required_controls.name: Validated archive and restore path
required_controls.description: Long-term object-storage archive for TMF documents and audit data; annual restore drill proving readability and integrity.

required_controls.name: Per-service validation evidence
required_controls.description: Each extracted service carries its own URS/FS/IQ/OQ artefacts and a traceability matrix, enabling independent releases.

compliance.validation_strategy: Risk-based CSA aligned with GAMP 5 and FDA CSA: Validation Plan approved by QA before Wave 1; Infrastructure IQ on the GxP landing zone; OQ scope targeted at changed functions (migrated Oracle schema and audit tables, extracted services, modernised identity flow); PQ via parallel run across one monitoring cycle for the replatformed monolith and each extracted service. Managed AWS services are treated as GAMP 5 Category 1 infrastructure, leveraging AWS supplier evidence. Change control and periodic review follow Annex 11 §10 and §16 across the subsequent extraction waves.
